prompt: A Redis started with no options reaches the memory of its machine. What happens?

choices.text: It evicts the least recently used keys
choices.why: With no `maxmemory` there is no ceiling to evict at.

choices.text: It refuses writes with an `OOM` error
choices.why: That needs a `maxmemory` to compare against; the default is 0, no limit.

choices.text: It grows until the kernel kills it
choices.why: Right. `maxmemory 0` means no limit inside Redis, so the only limit is the machine's.

choices.text: It moves the oldest keys to disk and keeps going
choices.why: Redis never swaps keys to disk on its own; persistence is a copy, not an overflow.

prompt: Under `noeviction`, a full instance refuses `SET product:KB-101 34990`. Which of these commands still works?

choices.text: `SADD tag:office KB-101`
choices.why: It could add data, so it is refused like the `SET`.

choices.text: `DEL page:1`
choices.why: Right. It frees memory, so Redis allows it; reads work too.

choices.text: `LPUSH viewed:ana MN-330`
choices.why: A push adds an element; refused.

choices.text: `INCR visits` on a key that does not exist yet
choices.why: It would create a key; refused.

prompt: A Redis container runs with `docker run --memory 1g` and `maxmemory 1gb`. Under load it disappears with exit code 137 instead of answering `OOM` errors. Why?

choices.text: Buffers and a fork's copy come on top of the data, and the kernel acts first
choices.why: Right. Set `maxmemory` well below the container's limit.

choices.text: Exit 137 is how Redis reports `OOM` to Docker when a write is refused at the ceiling
choices.why: 137 is a process killed by signal 9; Redis's own `OOM` is an error to a client, and the process lives.

choices.text: The units differ: `1g` in Docker is larger than `1gb` in Redis, so the limits never matched
choices.why: If anything Docker's is the larger; the gap that matters is what `maxmemory` leaves out.

choices.text: `noeviction` crashes Redis when it is full
choices.why: It refuses writes and keeps running, as the lesson's capture shows.

prompt: Under `allkeys-random`, the same load lost products that `allkeys-lru` kept. Why?

choices.text: A random pick gives a product read thousands of times the same chance as a page nobody reads
choices.why: Right. LRU uses the reads; random ignores them.

choices.text: `allkeys-random` evicts more keys in total
choices.why: All three evicted about the same number; only the choice differed.

choices.text: Products are larger than pages, and a random pick prefers large keys because they free more memory at once
choices.why: The products are a few bytes and random ignores size.

choices.text: Random evicts the newest keys, and the products were written last
choices.why: The products were written first, and random ignores age.

prompt: Match each policy to the keys it may evict and how it picks one.
hint: One description fits none of them.

pairs.right: any key, the one used least recently
any key, the one used least often
only keys with an expiry, the one closest to expiring

prompt: Every night at 03:00 a report reads every page in the cache once. Each morning the cache is slow until the popular product keys are rebuilt. Which change addresses it?
hint: What does one read do to each policy's idea of a key?

choices.text: Move from `allkeys-lru` to `allkeys-lfu`, which a single pass barely moves
choices.why: Right. Under LRU the pass makes every page recent; under LFU the products' counters still win.

choices.text: Move to `allkeys-random`, so the report's reads do not count
choices.why: Random ignores the report, and also every read the products ever had.

choices.text: Raise `maxmemory-samples` from 5 to 10
choices.why: Better sampling of LRU still evicts by recency, and the pages are the recent ones.

choices.text: Move to `noeviction`, so nothing is pushed out
choices.why: Then the cache refuses new entries when full, which is worse for a cache.

prompt: Redis evicts by sampling a few keys and evicting the best candidate among them. How many keys does it sample by default?
An instance runs `volatile-lru`. It is full, `evicted_keys` is 0, and writes fail with `OOM`. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: `volatile-lru` only evicts when `maxmemory-samples` is above 5
choices.why: Sampling decides which candidate, not whether eviction happens.

choices.text: No key filling it has an expiry, so none is a candidate
choices.why: Right, and Redis refuses writes as `noeviction` would. The lesson's run refused thousands of writes with nothing evicted.

choices.text: The keys are read too often to count as least recently used
choices.why: Something is always least recent; the problem is that nothing is eligible.

choices.text: `volatile-lru` needs the instance to have persistence on
choices.why: Eviction and persistence are independent settings.

prompt: One Redis holds rendered pages and the shop's stock counters, under `allkeys-lru`. What is the risk?

choices.text: Writes of new pages are refused once it is full
choices.why: `allkeys-lru` evicts instead of refusing.

choices.text: A stock counter nobody read for a while is evicted, silently
choices.why: Right. Every key is a candidate, and a record evicted is a record lost with no error.

choices.text: Pages are never evicted because they are larger
choices.why: Size plays no part; recency does.

choices.text: The counters lose their expiry when a page is evicted
choices.why: Evicting one key does nothing to another.

prompt: Which settings fit a Redis that holds only copies the application can rebuild?

choices.text: `noeviction` with snapshots and the append-only file
choices.why: That is the database column: it refuses when full and saves what nobody needs back.

choices.text: `volatile-ttl` with the append-only file
choices.why: It works only if every key has an expiry, and the log saves copies for nothing.

choices.text: `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu`, and no persistence
choices.why: Right. Any key may go, and a restart starts empty and fills again.

choices.text: `allkeys-random` with snapshots every minute
choices.why: Random throws away popular keys, and the snapshots cost forks for copies.

prompt: A team keeps one instance under `volatile-lru` for both cache pages and records. Which of these must hold for it to work? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Every cache write, in every service, sets an expiry
choices.why: Right. A cache key without one fills memory and can never be evicted.

choices.text: No record ever gets an expiry, even by accident
choices.why: Right. A record with an expiry becomes a candidate for eviction.

choices.text: The instance has the append-only file on
choices.why: Persistence is a separate question from what may be evicted.

choices.text: `maxmemory-samples` is raised to 10
choices.why: Sampling tunes accuracy; it does not decide what is eligible.

choices.text: A plain `SET` is never used to update a cache key
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12 showed that it removes the expiry.

prompt: `TTL cart:nobody` answers `-2`. What does it mean?

choices.text: The key exists and never expires
choices.why: That is `-1`.

choices.text: The key expired two seconds ago
choices.why: Negative answers are codes, not times.

choices.text: The key does not exist
choices.why: Right. `-1` is a key with no expiry; `-2` is no key.

choices.text: The key has an expiry but Redis cannot read it
choices.why: There is no such state.

prompt: A second after 200,000 keys expired, `DBSIZE` still counted many of them. Why?

choices.text: They leave when touched or sampled, not at the second they expire
choices.why: Right. Until then they are counted and take memory; a `GET` answers `(nil)` and deletes on the spot.

choices.text: `DBSIZE` is computed once a second and was out of date
choices.why: It is exact at the moment it answers; the keys really were still there.

choices.text: The keys had been made persistent by the `EVAL`, which sets no expiry on keys it writes
choices.why: Every key was written with `EX 1`, and all of them did go.

choices.text: Expiry waits for the next snapshot
choices.why: Snapshots have nothing to do with expiry.

prompt: A login service gives every session exactly `EX 3600`, and a marketing email brings 500,000 logins in ten minutes. What does the lesson suggest, and why?

choices.text: Shorten the expiry to 600, so that sessions are removed sooner
choices.why: They would still expire together, only sooner, and log people out.

choices.text: Add a few random seconds to each `EX`
choices.why: Right. Spread out, the active cycle never has a spike of dead keys to clear at once.

choices.text: Turn on `volatile-ttl`, so the sessions are evicted before they expire
choices.why: Eviction only runs at the memory ceiling; it does not spread expiry.

choices.text: Nothing: Redis removes each key at the exact second it expires
choices.why: It does not; the lesson's `DBSIZE` lagged behind expiry.

prompt: A key that exists but has no expiry answers `TTL` with ___.
On a cache, `evicted_keys` climbs steadily all day. What does it say?

choices.text: Expiry is working as intended
choices.why: That is `expired_keys`; eviction is a different counter.

choices.text: The cache is too small for what it is asked to hold
choices.why: Right. It keeps pushing out keys to make room.

choices.text: Keys are being deleted by the application with `DEL`
choices.why: `DEL` counts in neither counter.

choices.text: Persistence is failing
choices.why: That shows in `INFO persistence`, lesson 13.

prompt: The policy that keeps a small counter of how often each key is used, and evicts the key with the lowest, is `allkeys-___`.
Under `noeviction` with a 4 MB ceiling, the lesson sent 20,000 page writes and 17,668 answered `OK`. How many were refused?
A Redis that is the shop's only copy of its stock counters reaches its ceiling. Which policy keeps every counter, and what does the application see?

choices.text: `allkeys-lfu`; nothing, because popular counters survive
choices.why: An unpopular counter is still evicted, and it is a record that exists nowhere else.

choices.text: `noeviction`; `OOM` errors on new writes, which page somebody
choices.why: Right. A database refuses rather than forgets.

choices.text: `volatile-ttl`; nothing, because counters have no expiry
choices.why: With no candidates it refuses writes too, and its name promises an eviction that never happens.

choices.text: `allkeys-random`; occasional missing counters, rebuilt from the cache
choices.why: There is nothing to rebuild them from; this is the only copy.

prompt: A full instance under `volatile-lru` receives a `SET`. Put what Redis does in order.
items: Sample keys that have an expiry
Evict the least recently used of the sample
trap: Room is made before the command runs.

prompt: The shop's idempotency keys (`SET … NX EX 86400`) live in the same Redis as its page cache, under `volatile-ttl`. What can happen when it fills up?
hint: Do the idempotency keys have an expiry?

choices.text: Nothing: idempotency keys are never candidates
choices.why: They were written with `EX`, so under `volatile-` they are candidates like the pages.

choices.text: Writes are refused, because the keys have an expiry
choices.why: Keys with an expiry are what `volatile-` evicts; refusal comes when there are none.

choices.text: An idempotency key is evicted early, and a retried payment is charged twice
choices.why: Right. Pages with less time left go first, but they are records with an expiry, so the policy treats them as cache once the pages run short.

choices.text: The pages are evicted first because they are larger
choices.why: `volatile-ttl` picks by time left, not size; a page with an hour left goes after a key with less.
